But I for my part think the soldiers did this while there worked within them the invisible kings and princes of this world, who "stood by and came together in one against the Lord and against his Christ", so that that mockery of theirs may be seen to have been rather theirs than men's — and of those who in that dispensation did not know the wisdom of God, "for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty". Therefore that cohort was a mystery of some malignant host.

And they stripped him of his garments, which he had from above, the seamless tunic and the robe (for such does John describe his garments to be), and they clothed him (mocking him on account of his royal name) with a scarlet chlamys, not understanding what they do:

for that scarlet chlamys was a mystery of the scarlet sign which is written of in Joshua son of Nun, which that Rahab had for her salvation, and in Genesis, which was done upon one of the sons of Tamar at the hand of the one being born, that the scarlet should be bound as a sign of the future passion of Christ. Therefore now also the Lord, taking upon himself the scarlet chlamys, took upon himself the blood of the world,

and in that thorny crown he took upon himself the thorns of our sins woven into his head.

And concerning the chlamys it is written that they again stripped him of the scarlet chlamys, but concerning the thorny crown the evangelists wrote nothing of the sort, on account of which they wished us to seek out the outcome of the matter concerning the thorny crown, once placed on and never taken off. I therefore judge that that thorny crown was consumed from the head of Jesus, so that our old thorns are now no more, after Jesus once took them away from us upon his venerable head.

But if it is fitting to say something also about the reed which they placed in his right hand, we set forth a reasoning of this kind. That reed, then, was a mystery of a vain and fragile scepter, upon which we all leaned before we believed, a malignant scepter; for we trusted in the reed rod of Egypt or of Babylon or of whatever kingdom contrary against the kingdom of God.

And he took that reed and the rod of the fragile kingdom out of our hands, that he might triumph over it and crush it on the wood of the cross. And in place of that former reed, upon which we formerly reclined, he gave us the scepter of the heavenly kingdom

and the rod of which it is written: "the rod of equity is the rod of thy kingdom"; or a rod which may chastise those who have need of chastisement, of which the apostle says: "what will you? shall I come to you with a rod?" He gave us also a staff, that we might celebrate the Passover according to what is written: "let your staffs be in your hands", so that we might celebrate the Passover laying aside the reed rod which we had before we celebrated the Lord's Passover. But they strike with this fragile and vain reed the venerable head of Jesus, since that contrary kingdom also always reviles and beats God the Father — the head of the Lord the Savior. And in all these things the only-begotten power was not harmed, just as it also suffered nothing, though made "a curse for us", when by nature it was a blessing; but, being a blessing, it consumed and dissolved and dispersed every human curse.

(ubi sup.) Hence we understand what Mark means by clothed him with purple; (Mark 15:17.) instead of the royal purple, this scarlet cloak was used in mockery; and there is a shade of purple which is very like scarlet. Or it may be, that Mark spoke of the purple which the cloak contained, though its colour was scarlet.

(ubi sup.) But Matthew seems to introduce this here as recollected from above, not that it was done at the time Pilate gave Him up for crucifixion. For John puts it before. He is given up by Pilate.

(Quaest. Ev. ii. in fin.) That they took from off the Lord in His passion His own garment, and put on Him a coloured robe, denotes those heretics who said that He had a shadowy, and not a real body.

Or otherwise; The Lord having taken upon Him all the infirmities of our body, is then covered with the scarlet coloured blood of all the martyrs, to whom is due the kingdom with Him; He is crowned with thorns, that is, with the sins of the Gentiles who once pierced Him, for there is a prick in thorns of which is woven the crown of victory for Christ. In the reed, He takes into His hand and supports the weakness and frailty of the Gentiles; and His head is smitten therewith that the weakness of the Gentiles sustained by Christ's hand may rest on God the Father, who is His head.

Or otherwise, By the scarlet robe is denoted the Lord's flesh, which is spoken of as red by reason of shedding of His blood; by the crown of thorns His taking upon Him our sins, because He appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh. (Rom. 8:3.)

Or, The reed was a mystery signifying that before we believed we trusted in that reed of Egypt, or Babylon, or of some other kingdom opposed to God, which He took that He might triumph over it with the wood of the cross. With this reed they smite the head of Christ, because this kingdom ever beats against God the Father, who is the head of the Saviour.
This is to be understood to have been done at the end of all, when He was led off to crucifixion after Pilate had delivered Him up to the Jews.

It is to be noted, that when Jesus is scourged and spit upon, He has not on His own garments, but those which He took for our sins; but when He is crucified, and the show of His mockery is completed, then He takes again His former garments, and His own dress, and immediately the elements are shaken, and the creature gives testimony to the Creator.

Of the cloak it is mentioned that they took it off Him, but of the crown of thorns the Evangelists have not spoken, so that there are now no longer those ancient thorns of ours, since Jesus has taken them from us upon His revered head.

(Hom. in. Ev. xxxii. 3.) Or otherwise; By Simon who bears the burden of the Lord's cross are denoted those who are abstinent and proud; these by their abstinence afflict their flesh, but seek not within the fruit of abstinence. Thus Simon bears the cross, but does not die thereon, as these afflict the body, but in desire of vain-glory live to the world.
For a Jew was not worthy to bear Christ's cross, but it was reserved for the faith of the Gentiles both to take the cross, and to suffer with Him.

Let none think that John's narrative contradicts this place of the Evangelist. John says that the Lord went forth from the prætorium bearing His cross; Matthew tells, that they found a man of Cyrene upon whom they laid Jesus' cross. We must suppose that as Jesus went out of the prætorium, He was bearing His cross, and that afterwards they met Simon, whom they compelled to bear it.

Figuratively, the nations take up the cross, and the foreigner by obedience bears the ignominy of the Saviour.

For this Simon was not a man of Jerusalem, but a foreigner, and denizen, being a Cyrenean; Cyrene is a town of Lybia. Simon is interpreted 'obedient,' and a Cyrenean 'an heir;' whence he well denotes the people of the Gentiles, which was strange to the testaments of God, but by believing became a fellow-citizen of the saints, of the household, and an heir of God.

Or, as they went out, they laid hold of Simon, but when they drew near to the place in which they would crucify Him, they laid the cross upon Him that He might bear it. Simon obtained not this office by chance, but was brought to the spot by God's providence, that he might be found worthy of mention in the Scriptures of the Gospel, and of the ministry of the cross of Christ. And it was not only meet that the Saviour should carry His cross, but meet also that we should take part therein, filling a carriage so beneficial to us, ἀγγαρεία. Yet would it not have so profited us to take it on us, as we have profited by His taking it upon Himself.

And as they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; him they compelled to take up his cross.

For just as, according to the three evangelists, Jesus is tempted by the devil, but according to John (who made his discourse concern his spiritual nature) he is not tempted — for "the truth and the life" and "the resurrection" and "the true light" is not tempted, but he was tempted according to the man whom the only-begotten God had taken up — so according to John indeed the Savior, when those who had seized him laid it upon him, "bearing his own cross went out to the place which is called the place of Calvary", but according to the rest he does not bear it for himself.

For those who were leading him away to be crucified, as they went out, found a certain man of Cyrene, named Simon, whom they compelled to take up the cross of Christ. But it was fitting not only for the Savior to take up his own cross, but it was fitting also for us to bear it, fulfilling the compulsion that is salutary for us. Nor, again, would we have been to be profited so much by taking up his cross, as we are now profited by his cross, when he himself takes it up for himself and bears it.

But you will ask whether according to the text both things happened and the evangelists are not discordant with one another, and which of them happened first: that is, whether those who seized Jesus for crucifixion and laid the cross upon him, so that "bearing it" he might go out into the place of Calvary, did this first, before they compelled Simon of Cyrene — or whether, once they had gone out, they compelled Simon, but when they had come to the place in which they were going to hang him, they themselves placed the cross upon him, so that he himself might bear it. And whoever can examine this, let him examine it in inquiring into both cases, that he may find whether he received the completion of bearing the cross, or rather Simon of Cyrene, who was compelled not by chance, but according to some foreknowledge of God concerning him, led to this according to the disposition of God, so that he might be found worthy of the evangelical scripture and of the ministry of the cross of Christ, in which "the world is crucified" to the saints "and" the saints "to the world".

But certain persons have also wished to expound this very Simon of Cyrene morally, taking their occasion from the fact that he was from the Pentapolis of Cyrene in Libya, so as to say, from the five senses, that as it were the five senses bore the cross of that dispensation. And Simon is interpreted OBEDIENCE: but to whom did it more befit that he should bear the cross of Christ, than to obedience, or (as the second son of Leah was called) to Simeon? For among the Greeks both the patriarch and Peter are named in two ways (according to the property of the Hebrew tongue), so that it fits him who is so called that he be called both Simon and Simeon, since the Hebrews write both the name of Simeon and of Simon with the very same letters. And the place of Calvary is said to have no ordinary dispensation, in that there, where he who was to die for men was to die, he might die. For there has come to me a certain tradition of this kind, that the body of Adam, the first man, was buried there where Christ was crucified, so that "as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive"; that in that place, which is called the place of Calvary, that is, the place of the head, the head of the human race might find resurrection together with the whole people through the resurrection of the Lord the Savior, who there suffered and rose again. For it was unfitting that, while many born from him should receive remission of sins and obtain the benefit of the resurrection, he himself, the father of all men, should not rather obtain grace of this kind.

(Hom. de Cruc. et Lat. ii.) The Lord would not suffer under a roof, or in the Jewish Temple, that you should not suppose that He was offered for that people alone; but without the city, without the walls, that you might know that the sacrifice was common, that it was the offering of the whole earth, that the purification was general.
Such is the place of the cross, set up in the centre of the earth, that it might be equally free to all nations to attain the knowledge of God.

I have heard Calvary expounded as the spot in which Adam was buried, as though it had been so called from the head of the old man being buried there. A plausible interpretation, and agreeable to the ears of the people, yet not a true one. Without the city outside the gate are the places where criminals are executed, and these have got the name of Calvary, that is, of the beheaded. And Jesus was crucified there, that where the plot of criminals had been, there might be set up the flag of martyrdom. But Adam was buried near Ebron and Arbee, as we read in the volume of Jesus the son of Navec.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: And they gave Him gall to drink, and this to insult Him, but He would not. But another saith, that having tasted it, He said, "It is finished." And what meaneth, "It is finished?" The prophecy was fulfilled concerning Him. "For they gave me," it is said, "gall for my meat, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." But neither doth that evangelist indicate that He drank, for merely to taste differs not from not drinking, but hath one and the same signification.

And they gave him to drink wine mingled with gall. Mark says, mingled with myrrh. Matthew put gall (Mark 15:23.) to express bitterness, but wine mingled with myrrh is very bitter; though indeed it might be, that gall together with myrrh would make the most bitter.

And when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink. That Mark says, But he received it not, we understand to mean that He would not receive it to drink thereof. For that He tasted it Matthew bears witness; so that Matthew's, He could not drink thereof, means exactly the same as Mark's, He received it not; only Mark does not mention His tasting it.
That He tasted but would not drink of it, signifies that He tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again the third day.
Or, He therefore refused the wine mingled with gall, because the bitterness of sin is not mingled with the incorruption of eternal glory.

The bitter vine makes bitter wine; this they gave the Lord Jesus to drink, that that might be fulfilled which was written, They gave me also gall for my meat. (Ps. 69:21.) And God addresses Jerusalem, I had planted there a true vine, how art thou turned into the bitterness of a strange vine? (Jer. 2:21.)

And they gave him vinegar to drink mixed with gall; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink.

For it was enough for us that he should only taste it on our behalf, just as he tasted a death no longer than the span of three days, so also the vinegar mixed with gall. But another wine, not mixed with gall nor with any other contrary thing, he took and drank, and "giving thanks" he gave it to the disciples and promised that he would drink "it new in the kingdom" of God.

Yes, and besides the figure, there is contumely with ready lip, and dishonour, and infamy, and the ferocity involved in the cruel things which then disfigured and lacerated the temples of the Lord, that you may now be crowned with laurel, and myrtle, and olive, and any famous branch, and which is of more use, with hundred-leaved roses too, culled from the garden of Midas, and with both kinds of lily, and with violets of all sorts, perhaps also with gems and gold, so as even to rival that crown of Christ which He afterwards obtained. For it was after the gall He tasted the honeycomb and He was not greeted as King of Glory in heavenly places till He had been condemned to the cross as King of the Jews, having first been made by the Father for a time a little less than the angels, and so crowned with glory and honour.

On the other hand, Christ, who spoke not guile from His mouth, and who exhibited all righteousness and humility, not only (as we have above recorded it predicted of Him) was not exposed to that kind of death for his own deserts, but (was so exposed) in order that what was predicted by the prophets as destined to come upon Him through your means might be fulfilled; just as, in the Psalms, the Spirit Himself of Christ was already singing, saying, "They were repaying me evil for good; " and, "What I had not seized I was then paying in full; " They exterminated my hands and feet; " and, "They put into my drink gall, and in my thirst they slaked me with vinegar; " "Upon my vesture they did cast (the) lot; " just as the other (outrages) which you were to commit on Him were foretold,-all which He, actually and thoroughly suffering, suffered not for any evil action of His own, but "that the Scriptures from the mouth of the prophets might be fulfilled."

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: They parted the garments, by which such great miracles were done. But they wrought none now, Christ restraining His unspeakable power. And this was no small addition of insult. For as to one base and abject, as I said, and the vilest of all men; so do they dare to do all things. To the thieves at any rate they did nothing of the kind, but to Christ they dare it all. And they crucified Him in the midst of them, that He might share in their reputation.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: For after "they had mocked Him, they led Him to crucify Him," it is said, and when they had stripped Him, they took His garments, and sat down and watched Him, when He should die. And they divide His garments amongst them, which sort of thing is done in the case of very vile and abject criminals, and such as have no one belonging to them, and are in utter desolation.

(Hom. de Cruc. et Lat. ii.) He suffered on a lofty cross, and not under a roof, to the end that the nature of the air might be purified; the earth also partook a like benefit, being cleansed by the blood that dropped from His side.

It is to be noted, that this is no small degradation of Christ. For they did this as to one utterly abject and worthless, yet for the thieves they did not the same. For they share the garments only in the case of condemned persons so mean and poor as to possess nothing more.

(Lib. 83. Quæst. q. 25.) The Wisdom of God took upon Him man, to give us an example how we might live rightly. It pertains to right life not to fear things that are not to be feared. But some men who do not fear death in itself, yet dread some kinds of death. That no sort of death is to be feared by the man who lives aright, was to be shown by this Man's cross. For of all the modes of death none was more horrible and fearful than this.

(in Serm. non occ.) Let your holiness consider of what might is the power of the cross. Adam set at nought the commandment, taking the apple from the tree; but all that Adam lost, Christ found upon the cross. The ark of wood saved the human race from the deluge of waters; when God's people came out of Egypt, Moses divided the sea with his rod, overwhelmed Pharaoh, and redeemed God's people. The same Moses changed the bitter water into sweet by casting wood into it. By the rod the refreshing stream was drawn out of the rock; that Amalech might be overcome, Moses' outstretched hands were supported upon his rod; the Law of God is entrusted to the wooden ark of the covenant, that thus, by these steps we may come at last to the wood of the cross.

(de Cons. Ev. iii. 12.) Matthew shortly says, They parted his garments, casting lots; but John explains more fully how it was done. The soldiers, when they had crucified him, look his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat; now the coat was without seam. (John 19:23.)
Thus on the tree of life the salvation and life of all is suspended.
This which was now done to Christ had been prophesied in the Psalm, They parted my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture. (Ps. 22:18.)

And after they had crucified him, they divided his garments among themselves, casting lots, and sitting down they kept watch over him (27, 35. 36).

And there are even now those who indeed do not possess him, but possess his garments — the words set down in the Scriptures — and not even these in full but only in part, though the prophet foretold this very mystery which has now been fulfilled. But whether any of his garments was torn apart in that division, or whether each of them remained whole as it had been, and what kind those garments were, we do not read in the three evangelists; but in John we learn that "the soldiers, after they had crucified Christ, took his garments and made four parts, to each soldier a part, but the tunic, since it was not sewn together but woven from the top throughout the whole, they said to one another: let us not tear it apart, but let us cast lots for it". Not all of them, therefore, received it, but only the one who obtained it by lot. And if someone were to discuss the difference between those who possess the garments of the Lord, he will without doubt find that there are some who, in their doctrines, even though they do not possess him, nevertheless possess the "tunic" woven from the top "throughout the whole", while others possess not even this but only some small portion of his garment.

And consider this, that according to Matthew indeed Jesus, taking "vinegar mixed with gall", tasted it and "would not drink", but according to Mark, when "wine mingled with myrrh was given to him", "he did not take it".
It proceeds, And sitting down, they watched him there. This watchfulness of the soldiers and of the Priests has proved of use to us in making the power of His resurrection greater and more notorious.

And sitting down they kept watch over him there. And the soldiers indeed kept watch over the body, having been assigned by the chief priests, as though it were liable to be stolen away by his disciples if it were not guarded; but the divine dispensation raised him up and made not only two or three to be witnesses of his resurrection, but far more. For "he was seen by Cephas, then by the eleven, then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at once", "and last of all" by Paul. And it was no small sign of his resurrection, that he was seen by so many — by those who took up the danger of proclaiming him alive among the peoples who had demanded him for the cross. And now new chief priests (namely the sons of those chief priests) crucify the word of truth set down in the Scriptures by their false expositions, and slay it with lies; but the word of truth, because among them indeed it is slain yet lives in its own nature, always finds and chooses for itself vessels in which it may rise again and live and still confound its own slayers, shown by many testimonies to be alive.

And they set up over his head his accusation written, This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. I cannot sufficiently wonder at the enormity of the thing, that having purchased false witnesses, and having stirred up the unhappy people to riot and uproar, they found no other plea for putting Him to death, than that He was King of the Jews; and this perhaps they set up in mockery.

It was divinely provided that this title should be set up over His head, that the Jews might learn that not even by putting Him to death could they avoid having Him for their King; for in the very instrument of His death He not only did not lose, but rather confirmed His sovereignty.

The High Priest also in obedience to the letter of the Law wore on his head the writing, 'Holiness to the Lord,' but the true High Priest and King, Jesus, bears on His cross the title, This is the King of the Jews; when ascending to His Father, instead of His own name with its proper letters, He has the Father Himself.

And they placed above his head his charge written out: this is Jesus, the king of the Jews.

"Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed," and every script bears witness to his kingdom, whether of the Greeks or of the Romans or of the Hebrews, and for a crown above his head let there be written: this is Jesus, the king of the Jews, and let no other cause of his death be found (for indeed there was none), let this alone be held: that he was king of the Jews, concerning which he also spoke, saying: "but I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain"; and the chief of the priests indeed, according to the letter of the law, bore upon his head the shape of a sign, "the sanctification of the Lord" written on the plate, but the true chief of the priests and king, Jesus, on the cross indeed has written: this is the king of the Jews, yet ascending to the Father and receiving the Father into himself, in place of letters and in place of a name he has him who is named, and he has him as a crown, having been made worthy of him and made a house worthy of God the Father, he alone can sufficiently contain the Father.

Or otherwise; Two thieves are set up on His right and left hand, to signify that the entire human race is called to the Sacrament of the Lord's Passion; but because there shall be a division of believers to the right, and unbelievers to the left, one of the two who is set on His right hand is saved by the justification of faith.
As Christ was made for us a curse of the cross, so for the salvation of all He is crucified as guilty among the guilty.

(Serm. 55, 1.) Two thieves were crucified with him, one on the right hand and one on the left, that in the figure of His cross might be represented that separation of all mankind which shall be made in His judgment. The Passion then of Christ contains a sacrament of our salvation, and of that instrument which the wickedness of the Jews provided for His punishment, the power of the Redeemer made a step to glory.

(ap. Gloss. ord.) Or, by the two thieves are denoted all those who strive after the continence of a strict life. They who do this with a single intention of pleasing God, are denoted by him who was crucified on the right hand; they who do it out of desire of human praise or any less worthy motive, are signified by him who was crucified on the left.

Then they crucified with him two robbers, one on the right and one on the left.

The Lord, crucified among robbers like the robbers themselves, fulfilled the prophecy that says of him: "and he was reckoned among the wicked". And it is possible to see his disciples, giving testimony to the worship of God which was introduced through him, being reckoned "among the wicked" and being crucified with them, or enduring the remaining sufferings, just as those men did. For the world and the spirit that is in it always persecutes the highest men and punishes indeed the highest in wickedness for the benefit of the many, but the highest in virtue, because this world is not worthy of those who consider not "the things that are seen", but "the things that are not seen", and who despise it, just as also of old the saints walked "in sheepskins and in goatskins, destitute, afflicted, wandering in deserts, in mountains, and in caves, and in the dens of the earth, of whom the world was not worthy".
The thief who was saved may be a sign of those who after many sins have believed on Christ.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: But nevertheless not even here doth their contumely stop, but after having stripped and crucified Him, and offered Him vinegar, they proceeded still further, and beholding Him impaled upon the cross, they revile Him, both they themselves and the passers by; and this was more grievous than all, that on the charge of being an impostor and deceiver He suffered these things, and as a boaster, and vainly pretending what He said. Therefore they both crucified Him publicly, that they might make a show of it in the sight of all; and therefore also they did it by the hands of the soldiers, that these things being perpetrated even by a public tribunal, the insult might be the greater.

They revile him because they passed by that way, and would not walk in the true way of the Scriptures. They wagged their heads, because they had just before shifted their feet, and stood not upon a rock.

And as they passed by they blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying: aha, you who were destroying the temple and rebuilding it in three days; free yourself, if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. Likewise also the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and the elders and the Pharisees, said: he saved others, himself he cannot save; if he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross and we believe him. He trusts in God; he will free him now if he wills him; for he said, that I am the Son of God.

No one who stands blasphemes Jesus, nor anyone who walks aright; for it was those passing by who blasphemed him (or, as the Greek has it, those going past), who also, once the fence of the vineyard has been broken down by God, gather as their vintage those who have remained; for it is written: "Why have you cast down its fence, and all who pass by the way gather it as their vintage?" So long, therefore, as anyone has not passed by the way nor turned aside from the way, or, standing, can say to God: you have set "my feet upon a rock", he does not blaspheme Jesus; but if he has fallen or gone past or crossed over or turned aside, then he blasphemes him. As, further, those who have fallen into evil works, and those who have forsaken "the eternal bounds" and the way of the heavenly church, and are tossed and carried about "by every wind of doctrine in the deceit of men, in craftiness for the contriving of error". For if anyone should say that all heresies are passing by and turning aside, he will not sin, for which reason they too are counted among those passing by and blaspheme Jesus, having no firm head, but wagging it up and down, since they are not prudent nor have their eyes in their head, in which they ought to have had them, as the Preacher (Ecclesiastes) says: "the eyes of the wise man are in his head". It is, therefore, the work of those passing by and turning aside to blaspheme Jesus the Son of God, because "no one speaking in the Spirit of God says: anathema to Jesus".

Now there are various sayings of the blasphemers, one blasphemy of which is that which is uttered by those who neither understand nor hear the things that are said nor concerning what they make their assertions: for Jesus said: "destroy this temple, and I in three days will raise it up", but those passing by, as "false witnesses" against Jesus, said what had not been said concerning him, assailing him: aha, you who destroy the temple of God, and in three days rebuild it. For he does not himself destroy the temple, but what others destroy he himself builds; whether "the temple of his own body", which had been handed over to death by the Jews, or the temple of his witnesses and of all who had the word of God in them and died from the ambushes of the impious on account of their piety (for "the hour comes when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will rise again"). And not only in that which they said: he who destroys the temple, did they lie, but also in that which they said: "and I in three days will rebuild it". For neither did he say that he would rebuild the temple, but that he would raise it up; for the word of building does not indicate a sudden work, but the word of raising up does indicate it.

And those indeed who were deriding him said save yourself, but he (receiving power from the Father) both did this and more: for to all who receive his word he showed his salvation. And they indeed, deriding, said: if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, but he did not show himself the Son of God to those deriding him, yet he showed it to those believing in him, after he had dispensed the things which it behooved him to dispense in those three days, after, descending to the lower regions "put to death in the body but made alive in the spirit, he preached to the spirits who were in prison, who had not believed at some time, when the patience of God was awaited in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, in which few, that is eight souls, were saved through water". And he was not left there (as he himself said: "for you will not leave my soul in hell"), but it behooved him both to ascend to his own Father and God, that "ascending on high" he might take captivity captive and receive "gifts among men", and after these things show himself stronger than death, saying to it: "where, O death, is your sting?"

And likewise (while the rest were passing by and blaspheming him) the chief priests too and the scribes, themselves also passing by, said to him, overcome by the mighty works done by him before: he saved others, himself he cannot save (clearly not believing that he who was able to save others was much more able to save himself as well), and they promised that they would believe in him as in the King of Israel, if he were seen by them coming down from the cross. But he did not care to do anything unworthy on account of the injury of derision, nor to do what was being said by them apart from reason and order.

And as beginning to extenuate His former miracles, they add, Save thyself; if thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.

(Hom. de Cruc. et Latr. ii.) But He, on the contrary, does not come down from the cross, because He is the Son of God; for He therefore came that He might be crucified for us.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: And yet who would not have been moved by the multitude that was following Him, and lamenting Him? Nay, not these wild beasts. Wherefore also He to the multitude vouchsafes an answer, but to these men not so. For after having done what they would, they endeavor also to injure His honor, fearing His resurrection. Therefore they say these things publicly, and crucified thieves with Him, and wishing to prove Him a deceiver, they say, "Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days come down from the cross." For since on telling Pilate to remove the accusation (this was the writing, "The king of the Jews"), they prevailed not, but he persevered in saying, "What I have written, I have written," they then endeavor by their derision of Him to show that He is not a king.
What forgiveness then for them, when by the resurrection of His body they shall see the temple of God rebuilt within three days?
The foolish rabble cast the same taunt against Him that the false witnesses had invented, Aha! thou that destroyest the temple of God and rebuildest it in three days.

(Serm. 55. 2.) From what source of error, O Jews, have ye sucked in the poison of such blasphemies? What teacher delivered it to you? What learning moved you to think that the true King of Israel, that the veritable Son of God, would be He who would not suffer Himself to be crucified, and would set free His body from the fastenings of the nails? Not the hidden meaning of the Law, not the mouths of the Prophets. Had ye indeed ever read, I hid not my face from the shame of spitting; (Is. 50:6.) or that again, They pierced my hands and my feet, they told all my bones. (Ps. 22:16.) Where have ye ever read that the Lord came down from the cross? But ye have read, The Lord hath reigned from the tree.e
Aha! is an interjection of taunt and mockery.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q:
Wherefore they said those things, and also these. If "He is the king of Israel, let Him come down now from the cross. He saved others, Himself He cannot save," aiming hereby to bring discredit even on His former miracles. And again, "If He be Son of God, and He will have Him, let Him save Him."

O execrable; most execrable! What, were not the prophets prophets, nor the righteous men righteous, because God rescued them not out of their dangers. Nay surely they were, though suffering these things. What then could be equal to your folly? For if the coming of the dangers upon them did not injure their honor with you, how much more in the case of this man, was it wrong for you to be offended, when both by what He did, by what He said, He was ever correcting beforehand this suspicion of yours.

Yet nevertheless, even when these things were said and done, they prevailed nothing, not even at the very time. At any rate, he, who was depraved in such great wickedness, and who had spent his whole life in murders and house-breakings, when these things were being said, then confessed Him, and made mention of a kingdom, and the people bewailed Him. And yet the things that were done seemed to testify the contrary in the eyes of those who knew not the mysterious dispensations, that He was weak and of no power, nevertheless truth prevailed even by the contrary things.

Even the Scribes and Pharisees reluctantly confess that He saved others. Your own judgment then condemns you, for in that He saved others, He could if He would have saved Himself.

But unworthy of credit is that promise, And we will believe him. For which is greater, to come down while yet alive from the cross, or to rise from the tomb when dead? Yet this He did, and ye believed not; therefore neither would ye have believed if He had come down from the cross. It seems to me that this was a suggestion of the dæmons. For immediately when the Lord was crucified they felt the power of the cross, and perceived that their strength was broken, and therefore contrive this to move Him to come down from the cross. But the Lord, aware of the designs of His foes, remains on the cross that He may destroy the Devil.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: O execrable; most execrable! What, were not the prophets prophets, nor the righteous men righteous, because God rescued them not out of their dangers. Nay surely they were, though suffering these things. What then could be equal to your folly? For if the coming of the dangers upon them did not injure their honor with you, how much more in the case of this man, was it wrong for you to be offended, when both by what He did, by what He said, He was ever correcting beforehand this suspicion of yours.

At first both reviled Him, but afterwards not so. For that you should not suppose that the thing was arranged by any collusion, and that the thief was not a thief, he shows you by his wanton reproaches, that even after he was crucified he was a thief and a foe, but was afterwards totally changed.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87
q: Yet nevertheless, even when these things were said and done, they prevailed nothing, not even at the very time. At any rate, he, who was depraved in such great wickedness, and who had spent his whole life in murders and house-breakings, when these things were being said, then confessed Him, and made mention of a kingdom, and the people bewailed Him. And yet the things that were done seemed to testify the contrary in the eyes of those who knew not the mysterious dispensations, that He was weak and of no power, nevertheless truth prevailed even by the contrary things.

(de Cons. Ev. iii. 16.) It may seem that Luke contradicts this, when he describes one of the robbers as reviling Him, and as therefore rebuked by the other. But we may suppose that Matthew, shortly alluding to the circumstance, has used the plural for the singular, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we have, Hare stopped the months of lions, (Heb. 11:33.) when Daniel only is spoken of. And what more common way of speaking than for one to say, See the country people insult me, when it is one only who has done so. If indeed Matthew had said that both the thieves had reviled the Lord, there would be some discrepancy; but when he says merely, The thieves, without adding 'both,' we must consider it as that common form of speech in which the singular is signified by the plural.
That both the thieves cast in His teeth the manner of His Passion, shows that the cross should be an offence to all mankind, even to the faithful.

Or it may be said that at first both reviled Him; but when the sun had withdrawn, the earth was shaken, the rocks were rent, and the darkness increased, one believed on Jesus, and repaired his former denial by a subsequent confession.

Or, in the two thieves both nations, Jews and Gentiles, at first blasphemed the Lord; afterwards the latter terrified by the multitude of signs did penitence, and thus rebukes the Jews, who blaspheme to this day.

And the robbers who were crucified with him reproached him with the same thing.

And in commenting on John we have explained, as best we could, concerning the two robbers who were crucified with Christ, who according to Matthew indeed and Mark both reproached him on the cross, but according to Luke, who says that "one of the hanging robbers blasphemed him, saying: You are the Christ; save yourself and us. But the other, answering, rebuked him, saying: Do you not fear God, seeing that you are in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done nothing evil. And he said to Jesus: Remember me when you come into your kingdom. But Jesus, answering, said to him who had rebuked the one blaspheming: "Amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise".

It is fitting, therefore, that at first indeed both robbers should be understood to have blasphemed the Lord, but after this that one of them was converted and believed, pondering within himself both about these miracles which he heard had been done by him, and perhaps also seeing the change of the air and the darkness that came about, unusual and not such as was frequently accustomed to happen.

Or perhaps, as we said in that place too, these two robbers are different — of whom one was blaspheming him while the other rebuked the one blaspheming — and different were those two robbers who both blasphemed.

But that robber who was saved can be a mystery of those who after many iniquities believed in Christ and said: We have been crucified together with Christ and conformed to the death of Christ, and who always say to the Son of God: "Remember" us "when you come into your kingdom, and therefore" they are "in paradise" with him.
The thief who was saved may be a sign of those who after many sins have believed on Christ.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88
q:
This is the sign which before He had promised to give them when they asked it, saying, "An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign, and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas;" meaning His cross, and His death, His burial, and His resurrection. And again, declaring in another way the virtue of the cross, He said, "When ye have lifted up the Son of Man, then shall ye know that I am He." And what He saith is to this purport: "When ye have crucified me, and think ye have overcome me, then, above all, shall ye know my might."

For after the crucifixion, the city was destroyed, and the Jewish state came to an end, they fell away from their polity and their freedom, the gospel flourished, the word was spread abroad to the ends of the world; both sea and land, both the inhabited earth and the desert perpetually proclaim its power. These things then He meaneth, and those which took place at the very time of the crucifixion. For indeed it was much more marvellous that these things should be done, when He was nailed to the cross, than when He was walking on earth. And not in this respect only was the wonder, but because from heaven also was that done which they had sought, and it was over all the world, which had never before happened, but in Egypt only, when the passover was to be fulfilled. For indeed those events were a type of these.

And observe when it took place. At midday, that all that dwell on the earth may know it, when it was day all over the world; which was enough to convert them, not by the greatness of the miracle only, but also by its taking place in due season. For after all their insulting, and their lawless derision, this is done, when they had let go their anger, when they had ceased mocking, when they were satiated with their jeerings, and had spoken all that they were minded; then He shows the darkness, in order that at least so (having vented their anger) they may profit by the miracle. For this was more marvellous than to come down from the cross, that being on the cross He should work these things. For whether they thought He Himself had done it, they ought to have believed and to have feared; or whether not He, but the Father, yet thereby ought they to have been moved to compunction, for that darkness was a token of His anger at their crime. For that it was not an eclipse, but both wrath and indignation, is not hence alone manifest, but also by the time, for it continued three hours, but an eclipse takes place in one moment of time, and they know it, who have seen this; and indeed it hath taken place even in our generation.

And how, you may say, did not all marvel, and account Him to be God? Because the race of man was then held in a state of great carelessness and vice. And this miracle was but one, and when it had taken place, immediately passed away; and no one was concerned to inquire into the cause of it, and great was the prejudice and the habit of ungodliness. And they knew not what was the cause of that which took place, and they thought perhaps this happened so, in the way of an eclipse or some natural effect. And why dost thou marvel about them that are without, that knew nothing, neither inquired by reason of great indifference, when even those that were in Judaea itself, after so many miracles, yet continued using Him despitefully, although He plainly showed them that He Himself wrought this thing.

And from the sixth hour there was darkness over the whole earth until the ninth hour. From this text certain people malign the truth of the Gospel, saying: how can what is said be true according to the text, namely that there was darkness over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth, since no history records that this happened? And they say that, just as usually happens in an eclipse of the sun, so an eclipse of the sun occurred at that time.

Now an eclipse of the sun has always occurred throughout the ages at its own time. But the eclipse of the sun which is wont to happen according to the customary course of the seasons as they run does not occur at any other time than at the conjunction of the sun and the moon, when the moon, running beneath, obstructs the rays of the sun by coming to meet it, and by its encounter blunts its light. But at the time when Christ suffered it is manifest that there was no conjunction of the moon with the sun, since it was the Passover season, which is customary to keep when the moon has the fullness of the sun and is present the whole night.

How then could there be an eclipse of the sun, when the moon was full and had the fullness of the sun?

But certain believers, wishing to introduce some defense against these arguments, hard pressed by the words of those who professed such things, spoke thus: if no new portent had happened at the time of Christ's passion but everything according to custom, it would be believed that that eclipse of the sun had happened according to custom; but now, since it is established that the other portents which happened then did not happen according to custom, but were new and wondrous (for indeed "the veil of the temple was torn into two parts from top to bottom, and the earth quaked, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened and many bodies of the sleeping saints rose again"), it is manifest that that eclipse of the sun too, consequently, in keeping with the other new portents, happened contrary to custom. Again, against these things the "sons of this age" who are "wiser than the sons of light in their generation" say such things as this: grant that that eclipse of the sun happened contrary to custom at a time not ancient, under the rule of the Romans, so that darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour — how is it that no one of the Greeks, no one of the barbarians, recorded that so marvelous a thing had happened at that time, especially those who wrote and noted chronicles, whenever any such new thing ever happened, but only your authors have written this? And a certain Phlegon wrote in his Chronicles that it happened in the rule of Tiberius Caesar, but he did not indicate that this happened at the full moon.

See therefore whether this objection is not strong and able to move every wise man (who agrees neither with those who say these things nor with those who write those things, but hears everything with reason and judgment), and it is indeed not hard … and every one of the faithful (who indeed believes, yet does not believe with reason and with judgment), so that he may be so constant in faith that, even if they bring a thousand charges against the faith of the Gospel wishing to destroy our faith, he may in no part of them be shaken by the words of those who (pretending to believe the Gospel scriptures) through the occasion of one or another question, whether difficult or perhaps even insoluble, opposing the scriptures, hasten to take away the faith of Christ and of his Gospels from our soul, introducing certain moral matters and wishing to transfer the wonders accomplished by the power of God to certain secular customs. I have therefore judged it good, taking up the good purpose of those who desire to be constant in the faith, to find solutions to their accusations (as far as there is power in me from God) on behalf of the truth of the Gospel, so that the faithful may be fortified in faith not only by simple faith, but also by the reason of faith.

We say therefore that Matthew and Mark did not say that an eclipse of the sun then happened, and neither did Luke, according to very many copies which have it thus: "and it was about the sixth hour, and darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour, and the sun was darkened". But in certain copies it does not have: "darkness fell and the sun was darkened"; but thus: "darkness fell over the whole earth, the sun failing". And perhaps someone ventured (as though wishing to say something more manifest) to put, in place of: "and the sun was darkened", "the sun failing", supposing that the darkness could not have happened otherwise than by "the sun failing".

But I rather think that those who lie in wait for the Church of Christ altered this word, so that it read "darkness fell, the sun failing", in order that the Gospels might plausibly be refuted according to the contrivances of those wishing to refute them. I judge therefore that, just as the other signs which happened in his passion happened in Jerusalem only, so also the darkness was made over the whole earth of Judea only until the ninth hour. And the things I say happened in Jerusalem only are these: that "the veil of the temple was torn", that "the earth quaked", that "the rocks were split", that "the tombs were opened". For neither outside Judea "were the rocks split", nor "were tombs opened" other than only those which were in Jerusalem or perhaps in the land of Judea, nor did any other "earth quake" then except the earth of Jerusalem — for it is nowhere recorded that every element of the earth quaked at that time, so that (for example) both those who were in Ethiopia and those in India and in Scythia should feel it (which, had it happened, would without doubt be found in some histories of those who wrote in chronicles any new events). Just as, therefore, when it is said "the earth quaked", this refers to the earth of Jerusalem or (if one wishes to extend it more widely) to the earth of Judea, so also the darkness that fell from the sixth hour until the ninth over the whole earth was made over the whole earth of Judea, or certainly over Jerusalem only. Thus, therefore, whoever understands it this way understands it without fault, so that he may not, wishing to display the greatness of the miracle, fall into the mockery of the wise of "this age", and work unbelief rather than faith in wise men.

But someone says against these things: if the darkness then over the whole earth of Judea and Jerusalem was not made from an eclipse of the sun but from another cause, show the cause. To such we answer this: first indeed, that the evangelists did not at all name the sun in this place, but only that darkness fell over the whole earth. If therefore darkness fell over the whole earth with the sun not named, without doubt it follows to understand that certain most dark clouds, and perhaps not one but many and very great ones, ran together over the earth of Judea and Jerusalem to cover the rays of the sun, and therefore deep darkness fell from the sixth hour until the ninth. But since we have come to such a place, we say, lest perhaps also the "palpable darkness" in Egypt was made in this manner for "three days", not from an eclipse of the sun, but either because dark clouds ran together into one, or because the air there then became thicker over the Egyptians only — for "to all the sons of Israel", as the scripture testifies, "there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling".

For it is also impossible in an eclipse of the sun, which happens from the coming together of the moon to the sun, for darkness to be made for "three" continuous "days"; and it would be believed that there was some other cause of the darkness in Egypt, if the sun had even been named, or as though darkened at that time. But now the scripture of Exodus says nothing else except that "Moses stretched out his hand to heaven, and there was darkness and gloom and the rest over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days".

But as to my saying over the whole earth of Judea or Jerusalem, so that we may not understand every element of the earth, this is the proof, which is written in the third book of Kingdoms, where Obadiah the steward of Ahab said to Elijah: "what have I sinned, that you have given your servant into the hands of Ahab, that he may put me to death? As your God lives, if there is a nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you, and I said: he is not here, and he burned the kingdom and its regions, because he did not find you". For who would be so stony, reading these things, as to suppose that Ahab king of Israel sent into every nation of the world and into every kingdom of the whole earth seeking Elijah, and burned wherever it was said: Elijah is not here? But without doubt those things were said hyperbolically, showing that he sought him abundantly among the nations that were around Judea, according as he was able to seek. And we have said also in other places that, since two general creatures were made on the sixth day, first indeed the animals, and then man made "according to the image of God", it follows that that sixth day too should be understood as then having been divided into two kinds of creature, so that before the sixth hour the animals should be understood to have been created, but at the sixth hour the Lord said: "let us make man to our image" and made him then. … on which account it was fitting that, for the salvation of that same man, he who was dying should be hung up at that very sixth hour, and from the sixth hour for this reason the darkness should be made over the whole earth until the ninth. And just as, when Moses stretched out his hand "to heaven", "darkness was made over the Egyptians", who held the servants of God in servitude, an image of the future darkness which was to seize the Egyptians, similarly also when Christ at the sixth hour stretched out his hands on the cross to heaven over the people who had cried out: "take this man from the earth", and "crucify, crucify him", darkness was made, and they were deprived of all light.

And that darkness was an image of the future darkness which was to seize the Jewish nation, because they dared to lay their hands upon the true light.

Whence from that time all that nation has been filled with darkness, as the prophet says: "let their eyes be darkened that they may not see".

Likewise under Moses "there was darkness and gloom over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days; but to all the sons of Israel there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling". But under Christ darkness fell over the whole earth of Judea for three hours, but there was light over all the rest of the earth. Which everywhere illumines the whole Church of God in Christ.

And if until the ninth hour there was darkness over the whole earth of Judea, it is manifest that light shone upon them again, because "when the multitude of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved". But that the darkness was made over the whole earth of Judea for three hours, this shows that on account of their sins they were deprived of the light of three hours: of the light of God the Father and of the splendor of Christ and of the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Some take occasion from this text to cavil against the truth of the Gospel. For indeed from the beginning eclipses of the sun have happened in their proper seasons; but such an eclipse as would be brought about by the ordinary course of the seasons could only be at such time as the sun and moon come together, when the moon passing beneath intercepts the sun's rays. But at the time of Christ's passion it is clear that this was not the case, because it was the paschal feast, which it was customary to celebrate when the moon was full. Some believers, desiring to produce some answer to this objection, have said, that this eclipse in accordance with the other prodigies was an exception to the established laws of nature.

Against this the children of this world urge, How is it that of the Greeks and Barbarians, who have made observations of these things, not one has recorded so remarkable a phenomenon as this? Phlegon indeed has recorded such an event as happening in the time of Tiberius Caesar, but he has not mentioned that it was at the full moon. I think therefore that, like the other miracles which took place at the Passion, the rending of the veil, and the earthquake, this also was confined to Jerusalem. Or, if any one chooses, it may be extended to the whole of Judæa; as in the book of Kings, Abdias said to Elias, As the Lord thy God liveth, there is no nation or kingdom whither my lord hath not sent to seek thee, (1 Kings 18:10.) meaning that he had been sought in the countries round about Judæa. Accordingly we might suppose many and dense clouds to have been brought together over Jerusalem and Judæa, enough to produce thick darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour. For we understand that there were two creatures created on the sixth day, the beasts before the sixth hour, man on the sixth; and therefore it was fitting that He who died for the salvation of man should be crucified at the sixth hour, and for this cause that darkness should be over the whole earth from the sixth to the ninth hour. And as by Moses stretching out his hands towards heaven darkness was brought upon the Egyptians who held the servants of God in bondage, so likewise when at the sixth hour Christ stretched out his hands on the cross to heaven, darkness came over all the people who had cried out, Crucify him, and they were deprived of all light as a sign of the darkness that should come, and that should envelop the whole people of the Jews. Further, under Moses there was darkness over the land of Egypt three days, but all the children of Israel had light; so under Christ there was darkness over all Judæa for three hours, because for their sins they were deprived of the light of God the Father, the splendour of Christ, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. But over the rest of the earth there is light, which every where illumines the Church of God in Christ. And if to the ninth hour there was darkness over Judæa, it is manifest that light returned to them again after that; so, when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have entered in, then all Israel shall be saved. (Rom. 11:25.)

But My People hath changed their glory: whence no profit shall accrue to them: the heaven turned pale thereat" (and when did it turn pale? undoubtedly when Christ suffered), "and shuddered," he says, "most exceedingly; " and "the sun grew dark at mid-day: " (and when did it "shudder exceedingly" except at the passion of Christ, when the earth also trembled to her centre, and the veil of the temple was rent, and the tombs were burst asunder? "because these two evils hath My People done; Me," He says, "they have quite forsaken, the fount of water of life, and they have digged for themselves worn-out tanks, which will not be able to contain water.

And so the "pressure" must be maintained up to that hour in which the orb-involved from the sixth hour in a general darkness-performed for its dead Lord a sorrowful act of duty; so that we too may then return to enjoyment when the universe regained its sunshine. If this savours more of the spirit of Christian religion, while it celebrates more the glory of Christ, I am equally able, from the self-same order of events, to fix the condition of late protraction of the Station; (namely), that we are to fast till a late hour, awaiting the time of the Lord's sepulture, when Joseph took down and entombed the body which he had requested.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88
q: And for this reason, even after this He speaks, that they might learn that He was still alive, and that He Himself did this, and that they might become by this also more gentle, and He saith, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" that unto His last breath they might see that He honors His Father, and is no adversary of God. Wherefore also He uttered a certain cry from the prophet, even to His last hour bearing witness to the Old Testament, and not simply a cry from the prophet, but also in Hebrew, so as to be plain and intelligible to them, and by all things He shows how He is of one mind with Him that begat Him.

(de Trin. x. 50 &c.) From these words heretical spirits contend either that God the Word was entirely absorbed into the soul at the time it discharged the function of a soul in quickening the body; or that Christ could not have been born man, because the Divine Word dwelt in Him after the manner of a prophetical spirit. As though Jesus Christ was a man of ordinary soul and body, having His beginning then when He began to be man, and thus now deserted upon the withdrawal of the protection of God's word cries out, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Or at least that the nature of the Word being transmuted into soul, Christ, who had depended in all things upon His Father's support, now deserted and left to death, mourns over this desertion, and pleads with Him departing. But amidst these impious and feeble opinions, the faith of the Church imbued with Apostolic teaching does not sever Christ that He should be considered as Son of God and not as Son of Man. The complaint of His being deserted is the weakness of the dying man; the promise of Paradise is the kingdom of the living God. You have Him complaining that He is left to death, and thus He is Man; you have Him as He is dying declaring that He reigns in Paradise; and thus He is God. Wonder not then at the humility of these words, when you know the form of a servant, and see the offence of the cross.

He employed the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. (Ps. 22:1. Vulg.) That clause in the middle of the verse, Look upon me, is superfluous; for the Hebrew has only 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani,' that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? It is impiety therefore to think that this Psalm was spoken in the character of David or Esther or Mardocheus, when passages taken out of it by the Evangelist are understood of the Saviour; as, They parted my garments among them, and, They pierced my hands.

But it must be asked, What means this, that Christ is forsaken of God? Some, unable to explain how Christ could be forsaken of God, say that this was spoken out of humility. But you will be able clearly to comprehend His meaning if you make a comparison of the glory which He had with the Father with the shame which He despised when He endured the cross.

When He saw darkness over the whole land of Judæa He said this, Father, why hast thou forsaken me? meaning, Why hast thou given Me over exhausted to such sufferings? that the people who were honoured by Thee may receive the things that they have dared against Me, and should be deprived of the light of Thy countenance. Also, Thou hast forsaken Me for the salvation of the Gentiles. But what good have they of the Gentiles who have believed done, that I should deliver them from the evil one by shedding My precious blood on the ground for them? Or will they, for whom I suffer these things, ever do aught worthy of them? Or foreseeing the sins of those for whom He suffered, He said, Why hast thou forsaken me? that I should become as one that, gathereth stubble in the harvest, and gleanings in the vintage. (Mic. 7:1.) But you must not imagine that the Saviour said this after the manner of men by reason of the misery which encompassed Him on the cross; for if you take it so you will not hear His loud voice and mighty words which point to something great hidden.

Now about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani? that is: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? But those who were standing there and heard it said that this man is calling Elijah (27, 46. 47).

It must be inquired, in a manner worthy of the Lord, what that great voice of Christ was—whether great by reason of things signifying great mysteries, or great by the sensible and bodily hearing of a great voice. But I think that every voice of Christ, the Son of God, is great, even if it be soft; and Scripture bears witness to this very thing especially in those places in which it wishes to raise up the hearer, so that he may pass beyond that which many are able to understand in such passages, and may not remain in it (although according to the simple understanding it may have in it some truth), so that he may be able to understand something in a manner worthy on account of the great voice of the Lord. Since, therefore, by these words he shows that there is something hidden and great, when he cries out to God, saying, why hast thou forsaken me, therefore it must be inquired what it is that was forsaken by God. Christ; for it is not permissible to believe that he lies when he says: why have you forsaken me.

And some, out of a religious coloring on Jesus' behalf, and because they cannot explain what it means for Christ to be forsaken by God, suppose and say: it is indeed true what was said, yet it was said out of humility. But we, seeing him who had been established "in the form of God" descending from a greatness of this kind and emptying himself through this, that he "took on the form of a servant", and seeing in these things the will of him who sent him to such conditions, understand that, as regards those things in which there had been the form of the invisible God and the image according to the Father, he was forsaken by the Father when he "took on the form of a servant", and he was forsaken for the sake of men, so that he might take on such and so great things, so that he might come "even unto death", "and the death of the cross", which among men is seen to be the most shameful. For the extremity of his being forsaken came about when they crucified him and placed above his head, as if mocking him, letters saying: "this is Jesus the king of the Jews". And that too was an extremity of his being forsaken, that he was crucified among robbers, and that "those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads over him", and that the chief men with the scribes were saying: "he saved others, himself he cannot save", and still further that too, that "even the robbers reproached him" on the cross. Therefore you will be able clearly to understand what it is that he says: why hast thou forsaken me? — making a comparison of that glory which he had with the Father to the confusion which, despising it, he endured on the cross. For his throne was "as the sun in the sight of God, and as the perfect moon for ever; and his witness in heaven was faithful". But afterward, for those on whose behalf he says: why hast thou forsaken me, he added further, saying: "but thou hast repelled and brought to nothing, and hast put off thy Christ, thou hast overthrown the covenant of thy servant, thou hast profaned his holiness upon the earth", and the rest. And so long as there was light from the sun, even while enduring such great and such grievous things He did not say Why hast Thou forsaken Me?; but after He saw that darkness had come "over all the land of Judaea until the ninth hour," He said with His great voice Why hast Thou forsaken Me, wishing to show by these words this: that Thou hast forsaken Me willingly, Father, and hast delivered Me up, emptied out, to such calamities, in order that the people who had been held in honor with Thee might receive what it dared to do against Me — filling up the "measure of its fathers," and the things it did against the prophets — so that it might be deprived of the light of Thy watchful care and be brought into darkness, as though Thou, O God, wert now in no way present with them. But also for the salvation of the Gentiles Thou hast forsaken Me, that by the "trespass" of Israel there might come "the salvation of the Gentiles." Yet what so good a thing did those who believed from among the Gentiles do, that with My "precious blood" poured out upon the earth for them I should purchase them from the evil one who had held them fast? And why hast Thou "turned away Thy face, and I have become troubled," so that I say: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death"? Or what such worthy thing are those men going to do, for whom I suffer these things, that I should suffer these things for them? — even as the prophet also foretold beforehand concerning this very thing, as though crying out to Thee and saying: "What profit," Father, has been made to men "in My blood, while I go down into corruption? Shall the dust confess to Thee, or shall it declare Thy truth?" But perhaps also, seeing the sins of the men for whom He was suffering, He said: Why hast Thou forsaken Me, that I should become "like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like one who gleans grapes in the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat of the first-fruits?" And these things I say, "because the God-fearing man has perished from the earth, and there is none who sets right among men." Wherefore do not suppose that the Savior said these things after the manner of men, because of the calamity that had laid hold of Him upon the cross. For if thou takest it so, thou wilt not be one who hears the great voice in which He spoke these things, nor wilt thou seek things worthy of a divine voice. Therefore "the darkness indeed was made from the sixth hour over the whole earth until the ninth"; but before the ninth hour was ended, the Lord cried out about it with a loud voice, saying the things that are written, as if demanding that the sun of the earth should rise, dissolving in her the darkness of the three hours according to what we have set forth above.

We have, moreover, in that other Gospel a clear revelation, i.e. of the Son's distinction from the Father, "My God, why hast Thou forsaken me? " and again, (in the third Gospel, ) "Father, into Thy hands I commend my spirit.
He exclaims that God had forsaken Him. He commends His spirit into the hands of the Father.

However, if you persist in pushing your views further, I shall find means of answering you with greater stringency, and of meeting you with the exclamation of the Lord Himself, so as to challenge you with the question, What is your inquiry and reasoning about that? You have Him exclaiming in the midst of His passion: "My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me? " Either, then, the Son suffered, being "forsaken" by the Father, and the Father consequently suffered nothing, inasmuch as He forsook the Son; or else, if it was the Father who suffered, then to what God was it that He addressed His cry? But this was the voice of flesh and soul, that is to say, of man-not of the Word and Spirit, that is to say, not of God; and it was uttered so as to prove the impassibility of God, who "forsook" His Son, so far as He handed over His human substance to the suffering of death.

It follows, Some of them that stood by, &c.; some, not all; whom I suppose to have been Roman soldiers, ignorant of Hebrew, but from the words Eli, Eli, thought that He called upon Elias. But if we prefer to suppose them Jews, they do it after their usual manner, that they may accuse the Lord of weakness in thus invoking Elias.

But some standing there and hearing him said: This man is calling Elijah … but the others said: Let us see whether Elijah comes and delivers him.

As though they had heard that he called upon God, and had marveled at his prayer on the cross, greater than was the prayer of Jonah praying in the belly of the whale, and had been profited by it, so that even when set amid the most extreme calamities they might not cease to pray to God. And I say that the prayer of Christ was greater than that of Jonah in the belly of the whale on account of the magnitude of the things that are shown forth from it, and on account of the great effect of his voluntary passion.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88
q:
But mark herein also their wantonness, and intemperance, and folly. They thought (it is said) that it was Elias whom He called, and straightway they gave Him vinegar to drink. But another came unto Him, and "pierced His side with a spear." What could be more lawless, what more brutal, than these men; who carried their madness to so great a length, offering insult at last even to a dead body?

But mark thou, I pray thee, how He made use of their wickednesses for our salvation. For after the blow the fountains of our salvation gushed forth from thence.

Vinegar is wine, which has turned sour either from neglect, or the fault of the vessel. Wine is the honour of immortality, or virtue. When this then had been turned sour in Adam, He took and drunk it at the hands of the Gentiles. It is offered to Him on a reed and a spunge; that is, He took from the bodies of the Gentiles immortality spoiled and corrupted, and transfused in Himself into a mixture of immortality that in us which was spoiled.

Or otherwise; The Jews as degenerating from the wine of the Patriarchs and Prophets were vinegar; they had deceitful hearts, like to the winding holes and hollows in spunge. By the reed, Sacred Scripture is denoted, which was fulfilled in this action; for as we call that which the tongue utters, the Hebrew tongue, or the Greek tongue, for example; so the writing, or letters which the seed produces, we may call a reed.

And perhaps all who know the ecclesiastical doctrine, but live amiss, have given them to drink wine mingled with gall; but they who attribute to Christ untrue opinions, these filling a sponge with vinegar, put it upon the reed of Scripture, and put it to His mouth.

And immediately one of them ran up, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink. And thus he fulfilled in himself the prophecy that spoke of him: "and they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink". For this reason too, according to John, when Jesus had received the vinegar with the gall, he said: "it is finished" — this also, which the Scripture had foretold concerning me. And one may with pleasure apply this text against those who have written or do write malicious things against Christ, of whom Isaiah says: "woe to those who write malicious things; for in writing they write malicious things" (I speak of those who have left behind certain writings, speaking "iniquity on high"). And one will use this text when he sees them gathering from certain things they have heard — whether of heathen sayings or of barbarous discourses — and composing a narrative like a kind of sponge, filling it not with any drinkable word nor with wine that gladdens "the heart of man" nor with the water of "refreshment", but with a kind of contrary and harmful and undrinkable intelligible vinegar; and this sponge they put upon the reed of their own writing and (so far as in them lies) inflict injuries upon Jesus by a drink of this kind. And some indeed give Jesus "wine mingled with gall to drink", which Jesus the Son of God will not drink, but others give not wine but vinegar. And perhaps those who, so far as ecclesiastical doctrine is concerned, have right understanding, but live wickedly, give him "wine mingled with gall to drink"; while those who apply to Christ wisdoms alien from the truth, as though he were speaking them, these fill a sponge with vinegar, put it upon a reed, and give him to drink. But there are also those who, as John writes, "offer to his mouth both vinegar and gall". And perhaps those who merely have wrong understanding fill a sponge with vinegar and put it upon the reed of their own writing and give him to drink; but those who both understand wrongly concerning the dispensations of Christ and live wickedly, these, "putting a sponge full of vinegar with gall and hyssop" upon the reed of their writing, offer it "to his mouth". But he who will not even drink his "wine" because of the admixture of gall, will much more not drink "vinegar", nor "vinegar mingled with gall". Therefore let us, receiving from our Savior Jesus himself (who is the "true vine") wine pure from all sharpness and bitterness, wine which "gladdens the heart of man" and the heart of the Son of God himself, give him and his disciples to drink of it, so that he may say of us who give him and his disciples good drink: "I thirsted and you gave me drink". Let us also receive the "water of refreshment" with which "the good shepherd" nourishes the just, so that those who are fed by him may say: "he brought us up beside the water of refreshment".

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88
q: "And Jesus, when He had cried with a loud voice, yielded up the Ghost." This is what He said, "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again," and, "I lay it down of myself." So for this cause He cried with the voice, that it might be shown that the act is done by power. Mark at any rate saith, that "Pilate marvelled if He were already dead:" and that the centurion for this cause above all believed, because He died with power.

(de Fid. Orth. iii. 27.) Although He died as man, and His holy soul was separated from His unstained body, yet His Godhead remained inseparate from either body or soul. Yet was not the one Person divided into two; for as both body and soul had from the beginning an existence in the Person of the Word, so also had they in death. For neither soul nor body had ever a Person of their own, besides the Person of the Word.

(in Serm. non occ.) When now nought of suffering remains to be endured, death still lingers, knowing that it has nothing there. The ancient foe suspected somewhat unusual. This man, first and only, he found having no sin, free from guilt, owing nothing to the laws of his jurisdiction. But leagued with Jewish madness, Death comes again to the assault, and desperately invades the Life-giver. And Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost.
